title: The Shoes and the Lonely Oak
markdown:
In days long vanished, though the rain still knows the way, the town of Wobbly Shoelace went quiet. Cobblestones shone like wet stones. Puddles lay as wide as dinner plates and held the sky, so that anyone glancing down met a second, wobbling world looking back. Rooftops dripped a sleepy drip-drip-drip. It was the sort of afternoon that asked for a book, a lap, and nothing that needed hurrying.

Inside a shop that smelled of leather, beeswax, and old wood lived Ari, the cobbler’s daughter. Her fingers were quick as a squirrel’s paws at worn soles and leaky boots. She liked the moment when an old shoe felt brave again. On this splashy day she polished a pair of walking boots until they shone like toasted chestnuts, and she wished, without quite meaning to, that the rain might bring more than hush.

Her best friend Fizz was a boot-elf no bigger than her thumb. His own tiny boots went squeak-squeak whenever he hurried, a cheerful little tune he could not help. He took shining very seriously.

“Another rainy day, Fizz,” Ari said. It was not a sad voice. The rain drummed on the panes. Outside, the puddles doubled the grey and doubled her shop, and doubled Fizz as a bright speck on her shoulder.

“Gloomy for polish,” Fizz squeaked, nose twitching at the reflected sky.

Then a tap began that was not rain.

Tap. Tap. Tap.

A creak followed. A shuffle. A muffled thump, as if leather were stretching after a long sit.

“What’s that?” Ari whispered.

Fizz pointed a leather-gloved finger at the door. “The shoes. They’re moving.”

Through the rain-streaked glass, the farmer’s wellingtons took determined steps down the lane. That was the first answering of the wish: company, already on its way. Ari laughed, surprised, and then stopped laughing, because the farmer’s porch stood empty, and the mud at the gate had no boots left to belong to.

They pulled on cloaks. They could not let wellingtons wander into wet woods alone.

The tap-tap-tap wove a path between dripping trees. Moss sprang underfoot. The air smelled of dark earth, pine needles, and clean rain. Every leaf held a bead of water, and in each bead a tiny crooked oak stood upside down, tapping at a second sky.

Soon more shoes came, which pleased the hidden wisher and troubled the town. Baker’s slippers shuffled, flour still ghosting their toes. The mayor’s brogues clicked as if late for a meeting that had forgotten them. In Wobbly Shoelace, people padded in socks. The bakery smelled of worry as well as bread. Ari felt the second gift land: a crowd beginning, and a quiet unbalancing behind it.

“They’re all going to the woods,” Fizz said, wriggling with ticklish nerves. “The tapping is an invitation.”

“Then we go too,” Ari said. “They might catch a chill. They might forget the way home.”

Deeper in, the last of the town’s shoes arrived, baby boots no bigger than Ari’s palm wriggling their laces as if proud to be included. That was the third answering: every pair, every size, a whole court of leather and cloth around a grand oak whose branches reached up like the kindly fingers of a giant. Its trunk was as wide as three grown people hugging. In a crevice of a thick, weathered branch sat a very old acorn. Every few moments it tapped the bark.

Tap. Tap. Tap.

The shoes stood still, soles pressed to moss, laces tidy. Some looked confused, tongues lolling. Others creaked, as if sad without knowing why. Ari crept closer with Fizz like a brave captain on her shoulder. The puddles at the roots showed her face, Fizz’s, and the oak’s dark crown, all mixed together. She understood then. The tapping was not a command. It was a plea.

“Why are you tapping, little acorn?” she asked, voice as soft as a moth.

The acorn stopped. The woods held their breath. A voice like a thousand autumn leaves came from the oak itself.

“I am lonely. For years I have watched sun and rain with no one to hear my leaves. So I wished into the wet world. The wet world is a mirror, and a mirror will fetch what you ask, if you tap long enough.”

The oak had been granted what it yearned for. The shoes had come. They could stay forever, a silent ring of polish and rain, and still not be listeners. They were absences wearing laces. If they never went back, Wobbly Shoelace would be the lonely one, and the oak would have only empty leather for company.

Ari thought of the smiles when she mended a boot — not because the boot stayed in the shop, but because it went walking and came home.

“You poor oak,” she said. “You don’t have to be lonely. But if they never go back, the town will miss its feet, and you will still be talking to the insides of shoes.”

Fizz scurried up the bark, tiny boots finding holds. “These shoes have stories in their soles. Puddles jumped. Hills climbed. They can visit. Visiting is a kind of staying.”

The oak rustled, a sound like a question learning to be a sigh. Then it spoke a couplet, old as rain:

“Come rest, come share the dripping day —
Then walk your people home, I pray.”

The assembled shoes shuffled. They settled at the roots as if trying the idea on. Ari sat. Fizz sat. The oak told of a summer when a wren nested in the crook that now held the acorn, and of a winter when ice made every twig a quiet bell. The shoes warmed. When the tale rested, the wellingtons turned first, as if they had a field to get back to. Slippers followed. Brogues clicked a polite goodbye. The baby boots wiggled, then toddled after, very pleased with themselves.

The acorn tapped once more.

Tap.

This time it sounded like thanks.

From that day the town’s shoes did not vanish into the woods. On wet afternoons they came, rested, heard a season or two, and went home shining. The puddles still held the sky. Ari and Fizz often sat beneath the oak with well-behaved shoes all around them, and the tapping — which had been a lonely wish — became a welcome, then a goodbye, then a welcome again.
